clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: Piano music that is trying to be water. Big quiet chords drop like a pebble, then the surface breaks into ripples — pentatonic figures, whole-tone haze, parallel chords sliding around instead of resolving.

clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: It's the first piece in a 1905 piano set. The other two are a slow tribute to an old claveciniste and a running, almost toccata-like movement.

clues.label: A historical event connected to the composer
clues.text: At the Universal Exposition of 1889 he heard a Javanese gamelan for the first time — and he was still talking about it years later.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: He trained at his country's Conservatoire and won the Prix de Rome. Then he got to Italy, hated the residency, and left early.

clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: His most famous piano piece is the moonlight one — Clair de lune. His most famous orchestra piece is about a faun's afternoon. If you have ever put on a 'relaxing classical' playlist, you have already heard him.

explanation.summary: Water on the piano, the 1889 gamelan, and Clair de lune: Claude Debussy, writing Reflets dans l'eau in France in 1905.

points.text: Those pebble-chords and rippling pentatonic figures are the opening of Reflets dans l'eau, the first piece of Images, Book I.
The set is Images: Reflets dans l'eau, Hommage à Rameau, then Mouvement.
The Exposition was the Paris one of 1889, for the centenary of the Revolution. The gamelan stuck with him.
The Conservatoire is the one in Paris, and the Prix de Rome is the official stamp of the French system — even if he couldn't wait to leave Italy.
Clair de lune and Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune. If you know two Debussy pieces, it's these.
